Northern Alaska Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Fairbanks AK
128 PM AKDT Thu Oct 8 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...
Central and Eastern Interior...
- Drier weather for Thursday through Saturday.

- A warming trend begins Friday and lasts through the weekend, 
  before cooler weather returns early next week.

- Gusty south winds develop through the AK Range late Friday. 
  Gusts peak upwards of 60-70 mph on Saturday. 

West Coast and Western Interior...
- The main story is a Bering Sea low which will bring strong
  wind and minor coastal impacts Thursday into Friday. Before
  slowly weakening through the weekend. More elaboration about 
  the coastal impacts in the coastal section.

- South/southeast winds increase through Thursday. Maximum wind
  gusts are expected to be between 45 and 65 mph, with the 
  strongest winds expected offshore.

- Multiple rounds of precipitation are expected, with the bulk 
  of it on Friday. Precipitation will be mostly rain for the 
  southern half of the West Coast and mostly snow for the 
  northern half.

- 5" to 10" of snow expected in the higher terrain North of the
  Kobuk Valley. Elsewhere, 2" to 4" can be expected.

North Slope and Brooks Range...

- Temperatures continue to remain cold with highs in the 20s and
  lows in the upper single digits to low teens.

- Strong south/southeast winds increase across NW Arctic Coast
  with gusts up to 60 mph likely on Friday. Periods of rain
  likely along the Chukchi Sea Coast Friday/Saturday with snow
  in the Western Brooks Range. Totals of 5-10 inches in the 
  Western Brooks Range.

- Snow spreads east Friday and Saturday, but accumulations will
  be much lighter along the coasts, generally less than an inch.

- Southerly winds increase on Saturday with gusts upwards of 45
  mph possible in Atigun and Anaktuvuk Passes and 30 mph along
  the Arctic Coast. 

&&

.SYNOPSIS...
A large storm in the Western Bering Sea dominates the weather
through the end of the week. This storm brings strong
east/southeast winds, periods of moderate to heavy
precipitation, and high water levels to the West Coast.
Relatively dry conditions in the Interior through Friday with
gusty southerly winds through the Alaska Range Passes.

&&

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY/...
At the start of the forecast period Thursday, a strong storm
system in the Bering Sea dominates the weather for the end of
the week. As of Thursday morning, the low rotates in the
northwestern Bering Sea with a strength around 944 millibars.
The Eastern portions of the state sit under a ridge of high
pressure. A front extending from the low is expected to sweep 
across the West Coast from south to north Thursday through early
Friday morning. This front is expected to be the most intense 
part of the storm for much of the West Coast. Strong south to 
southeast winds, a band of moderate to heavy precipitation, and 
higher water levels leading to high surf and minor flooding 
impacts are all associated with this initial front. 

The storm weakens steadily while it very slowly meanders towards
the West Coast. By midday Friday, the low will have weakened to
around 968 millibars in roughly the same location as Thursday.
By midday Saturday, it will have weakened to around 979
millibars while only having moved slightly east of its position
Thursday. By midday Sunday, it will have weakened further
towards around 985 millibars and will have finally started
moving east towards the West Coast. By this point the storm will
be significantly weaker and less organized than it was Thursday.
Impacts from the storm, especially wind and high water,
therefore gradually weaken over the weekend following the
initial spike with Thursday's frontal passage. 

Away from the coast, the higher pressure to the east is one of 
the main factors limiting the storm's eastward progression.
Mostly clear and dry conditions are expected across much of the
Central and Eastern Interior and most of the North Slope through
Friday under this higher pressure. As the low pushes against the
high and attempts to push fronts farther inland, southerly flow
develops aloft across the Interior and West Coast. This
southerly flow helps to reinforce the drier air over the
Interior through downslope heating/drying and brings gusty
southerly winds to the Alaska Range Passes. As the high and low
weaken each other, the pressure gradient weakens which weakens
the southerly flow. As the high weakens, precipitation from the
low is able to reach farther east into the Central Interior by
late Friday/early Saturday and into the Eastern Interior by
Sunday.

&&

.LONG TERM /SUNDAY NIGHT THROUGH THURSDAY/...
At the start of the long term forecast period, late Sunday, the
low which has been the main focus of the short term forecast 
period will have weakened to around 990 millibars and have
shifted to the northeastern Bering Sea near St. Lawrence Island.
The low will have overtaken Northern Alaska with chances of rain
and snow across the entire region. Winds will have weakened
significantly as the pressure gradient weakened. Light to
moderate mostly easterly winds with chances of rain and snow 
continue through early next week. 

Tuesday into Wednesday,another low moves east across the North 
Pacific just south of the Aleutians and strengthens. As it 
strengthens Wednesday, it pulls the remnants of the Bering Sea 
low into itself and becomes the new base of a broad trough 
encompassing almost all of Alaska. There remains considerable
disagreement in the exact location and strength of this next low
pressure system, but all models are indicating that it will
remain south of Northern Alaska. The northernmost solutions pull
it into Bristol Bay which would bring strong north/northeasterly
winds and additional rain/snow to the West Coast, especially
south of the Bering Strait. More southern solutions keep the low
south of the Alaska Peninsula which significantly limits any
impacts for Northern Alaska.

Coastal Hazard Potential...
As of Thursday morning, a strong low pressure system spins in 
the Western Bering Sea. A front from this system pushes north
through Thursday bringing strong south/southeasterly winds to
the West Coast. For most locations water levels peak for the 
event with the frontal passage Thursday. Coastal flood 
advisories are in effect for the Bering Strait Coast, Southern 
Seward Peninsula Coast, and Hooper Bay for water levels peaking 
at 4 to 6 feet above the normal high tide line with the Thursday
high tide(s). Elsewhere high surf is expected with water levels
peaking 2 to 4 feet above the normal high tide line. 

Water levels lower Friday before rising slightly Saturday into
Sunday. These levels are lower than the Thursday peak, with the
Southern Seward Peninsula and Hooper Bay closer to 2 to 4 feet
above normal and the rest of the coast closer to 1 to 3 feet
above normal. These weekend water levels slowly lower as the low
in the Bering Sea weakens through the weekend.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...
No concerns at this time.
